extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians of mathematics, and historians of science (conference participants and interested scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Conference report and set of abstracts about the history of mathematics (roughly turn of 20th century to 1950) organized around the theme of 'transition.' Presents methodological reflections and case studies useful for historians evaluating disciplinary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition as a historiographical category
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition as a historiographical category is nothing inherent in the sequence of events studied, but a product of this reflection: 'The historian fabricates transitions with all their elements: the ‘before,’ the ‘moment’ of transition, and the ‘afterwards.’'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'transition' as an interpretive construct to be justified; make explicit how you demarcate 'before', 'moment', and 'afterwards' rather than assuming they are self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diverse documentary evidence to describe a domain's state
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe the state of a mathematical subdiscipline, combine multiple types of sources: reports that documented (and shaped) the domain, monographs, and production registers (e.g., Zentralblatt subject registers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The talk on algebraic geometry lists concrete exemplars (Brill & Noether, Castelnuovo & Enriques, major monographs, and Zentralblatt entries). Use a mixture of published reports, textbooks/monographs, and bibliographic/abstracting service data to characterize practice and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unhelpful national labels (e.g. 'Italian school')
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to identify 'typically Italian' notions or methods is problematic; it can be advisable to ban the epithet 'Italian' from the historical investigation insofar as it may carry unwarranted connotations like 'intuitive' or 'loose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with nationality-based labels: examine social networks, publication venues, and methodological commonalities rather than relying on national stereotypes; consider internal diversity and political pressures (e.g., Severi's fascist turn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify external challenges and rival research agendas
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand transitions within a field, identify the rival agendas and criticisms coming from outside a dominant school (examples: Zariski’s criticism of Severi, van der Waerden’s algebraization, Deuring/Weil’s notions), since these challenges can precipitate re-foundational change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map key critical publications, polemics, and alternative programs as drivers of transition; document timing and intellectual content of these rivalries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse actors' time horizons
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the various actors’ time horizons — how they projected themselves into the future at various points of the process (e.g., Zariski had no re-foundational project before 1937; van der Waerden favored a mild algebraization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess participants' programs and aspirations over time: who sought incremental change versus radical re-foundation? Use letters, prefaces, and programmatic writings to read time-horizon ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse geographical and geopolitical constellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account the changing geographical/geopolitical constellation (e.g., emigrations, formation of research axes such as Rome–Berlin, relocations to the US) as these materially and culturally shape transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track migrations, institutional moves, and geopolitical disruptions (wars, expulsions) and relate them to shifts in research practice and community formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse conceptual shifts (classical → abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the passing from a 'classical' to an 'abstract' point of view as a central dimension of transition (comparison made with axiomatization in probability and the resistance to formal definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document new axioms, definitions, or formal frameworks; show how authors reinterpreted earlier intuitive concepts within abstract algebraic/axiomatic frameworks (examples: Weil, Zariski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to style and presentation as markers of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of style (presentation, mannerisms) can gain importance when substantive novelty is scant; stylistic changes in exposition may signal new practices (e.g., Weil’s mannerisms heralding a new way of doing algebraic geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare expository choices, textbook organization, and rhetorical strategies across generations to detect shifts in epistemic norms and acceptable forms of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Kuhn-like paradigm-shift pattern cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of transition may follow a pattern reminiscent of Kuhn’s paradigm shift (e.g., Zariski’s and Weil’s works ushering in new practices), but this analogy should be applied cautiously and not uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Kuhn as a heuristic, checking for anomalies, crisis, and eventual institutionalization of new practices rather than assuming a strict Kuhnian model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field consolidation signaled by textbooks and codification
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject becomes a recognizable theory when textbooks codify methods, define its distinct methods, and provide reasons for studying it (example: early textbooks on complex function theory created the subject by establishing methods like the residue theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey textbook literature, editions, and their emphases; the emergence of a large textbook corpus (dozens over decades) indicates consolidation and teaching norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate mathematical-practice change via formalization/algebraization
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect transitions in mathematical practice by identifying moves to 'algebraize' or 'arithmetize' formerly geometric/analytic domains (examples: Kähler’s use of differential forms and differential ideals; Ritt’s algebraic treatment of DEs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace introduction and uptake of new tools (exterior calculus, differential ideals, algebraic methods) and how they reframe problems; document follow-up literature and reviews assessing impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-terminology / method take-up as evidence (e.g., differential forms, differential ideals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific technical innovations (like Kähler’s use of the associative ring Ω of differential forms, exterior multiplication, operation d with ddω = 0, and the notion of 'differential ideals' closed under d) are markers of new practice in DE theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing intellectual change, cite the technical definitions and theorems that signal a novel toolkit and show which later authors built on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate foundational debates by philosophical and applied connections
rubrics_metrics.description: In foundational debates (e.g., probability: von Mises’ frequency theory vs later measure-theoretic axioms), evaluate both the philosophical stance and the degree to which formulations connect to practice and practitioners (physicists, engineers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document axiomatic claims, methodological commitments (positivism, frequency vs Bayesian vs measure-theoretic), and the extent to which proposals addressed practical modelling needs (von Mises’ emphasis on practitioners and Stieltjes integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess influence by failure modes and institutional interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for reasons why a figure’s influence may fade (e.g., von Mises' partial inability to manage logical implications of notions he introduced; his expulsion in 1933), as part of evaluating their role in transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include biographical and institutional disruptions (expulsions, war, exile) as causal factors in why certain approaches did or did not consolidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple archival and non-academic sources in biographical reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographical work should combine family testimony, archival holdings (personal papers, institutional files), patent/industrial archives, and contemporary records (e.g., Zentralblatt employment or Habilitation committees) — as in the Heegner example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference family documents, institutional archives, patent records, and oral histories; note where archives (e.g., Telefunken) illuminate non-academic activities that affected a mathematician’s life and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace cross-disciplinary and application-driven interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying transitions, trace how mathematics interacted with other fields (physics, engineering, ballistics, probability applications) since these connections often stimulated new methods and institutional agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document collaborations, citations, and applied problem domains that motivated mathematical advances (e.g., probability’s wartime uses, Kähler’s applications to mathematical physics).
